exercises.passage:
Learn While You Earn

For many school-leavers, university feels like the only path to a good career. Apprenticeships offer a different route: young people work for a real employer while studying toward a recognized qualification. Instead of paying tuition fees, apprentices earn a salary from the first month, and the employer usually covers the training costs.

The model works best when the classroom learning connects directly to daily tasks. An apprentice electrician, for example, may study circuit theory in the morning and install wiring in the afternoon. This combination helps knowledge stick, because every new idea is tested in practice the same week it is taught.

Apprenticeships are not an easy option. The workload is heavy, combining a full job with evening study, and some programs pay modest wages at the start. Still, for students who prefer doing over memorizing, the mix of income, experience, and a qualification without debt can be difficult to beat.

questions.explanation: The first paragraph contrasts apprenticeships with university: apprentices earn a salary while employers cover training.
options: Apprentices receive no pay during training.
Apprentices earn money while their training is usually paid for.
Apprentices study full-time before starting work.
Apprentices must pay their own tuition fees.
questions.question: What is one financial advantage of an apprenticeship mentioned in the passage?

questions.explanation: The electrician example shows morning theory applied to afternoon wiring work in the same week.
options: Trainees repeat the same task every day.
Classroom study happens only after two years of work.
New ideas from class are quickly tested in real tasks.
Theory exams replace all practical work.
questions.question: According to the passage, why does the combination of study and work help learning?

questions.explanation: The final paragraph lists heavy workload and modest starting wages as real difficulties, so the writer's view is balanced.
options: It admits real difficulties alongside the benefits.
It claims every apprentice becomes wealthy quickly.
It argues university is always the better choice.
It ignores any negative side of apprenticeships.
questions.question: What can be inferred about the writer's attitude toward apprenticeships?

exercises.passage:
Heavy Bags, Light Screens?

Many schools are replacing printed textbooks with digital versions on tablets and laptops. One clear benefit is cost and weight: a single device can hold every book a student needs for the year, and updates can be added without printing thousands of new copies. For schools with limited budgets, this difference matters.

However, teachers report mixed results. Some students read faster on paper and remember more of what which they read, possibly because physical pages make it easier to return to a difficult paragraph. Screens also bring distractions. Messages, games, and videos are only one tap away, and long reading sessions can cause tired eyes.

The most successful schools do not treat the choice as all or nothing. They use digital books for subjects that change often, such as technology and current events, while keeping printed books for long novels and exam preparation. The device is a tool, and like any tool, its value depends on how carefully it is used.

questions.explanation: The first paragraph names cost, weight, and easy updates as the benefits of digital books.
options: Digital books improve eyesight.
Digital books remove all distractions.
Digital books are always cheaper for families.
Digital books save weight and are easy to update.
questions.question: What is one benefit of digital textbooks mentioned in the passage?

questions.explanation: The passage says physical pages may help because students can easily return to a difficult paragraph.
options: Paper books are always free.
Paper pages make it easier to revisit hard sections.
Paper books update themselves automatically.
Paper books prevent all tiredness.
questions.question: Why might some students remember more when reading on paper?

questions.explanation: The final paragraph recommends digital for fast-changing subjects and print for novels and exams.
options: Ban all devices from schools.
Give every subject only digital books.
Mix formats depending on the subject.
Stop buying books of any kind.
questions.question: What approach does the writer recommend?

exercises.passage:
Beyond 'Good Job'

Most students have received feedback that says little more than 'good job' or 'needs improvement.' These comments feel safe, but they give the learner almost nothing to act on. Effective feedback looks different: it points to one specific part of the work, explains what worked or failed there, and suggests a concrete next step.

Timing matters as much as content. A comment on an essay returned three weeks later arrives when the student has already forgotten the thinking behind it. Short feedback given within a day or two usually changes the next piece of work more than a long report delivered late. Even two sentences are enough.

Students also need a chance to use the advice. Teachers who build ten minutes of revision time into the next lesson let learners apply the comment immediately, turning feedback from a final judgment into part of the learning process itself.

questions.explanation: The first paragraph says vague comments give the learner almost nothing to act on.
options: They give learners almost nothing specific to act on.
They are too long for students to read.
They always contain incorrect information.
They are never positive enough.
questions.question: What is the problem with comments like 'good job'?

questions.explanation: The passage states that late feedback arrives after the student has forgotten their thinking.
options: It is always too positive.
It focuses only on grammar.
It is written too quickly.
It arrives after students forget their thinking.
questions.question: Why is late feedback less useful?

questions.explanation: The final paragraph says revision time lets learners apply the comment immediately.
options: It shortens every lesson.
It lets students apply advice right away.
It removes the need for teachers.
It replaces all homework.
questions.question: What is the purpose of revision time in the next lesson?

exercises.passage:
Let Teenagers Sleep

Asking a sixteen-year-old to solve algebra at half past seven in the morning ignores biology. During puberty, the body clock shifts later: teenagers naturally feel sleepy later at night and need to sleep later in the morning. A schedule that suited a ten-year-old can leave an older student permanently short of rest.

The effects go beyond yawning in class. Studies link short sleep in teenagers to weaker concentration, lower mood, and more frequent illness. Some school districts that moved start times later by even one hour reported better attendance and calmer morning lessons within a single term.

Change is not simple. Bus timetables, parents' working hours, and after-school sports all depend on the current schedule. Still, the evidence points in one direction: when schools treat sleep as part of learning rather than an obstacle to it, students arrive more ready to learn.

questions.explanation: The first paragraph explains that puberty shifts the body clock later.
options: Teenagers dislike all school subjects.
Teenagers need less sleep than adults.
Teenagers' body clocks naturally shift later.
Teenagers prefer studying at dawn.
questions.question: Why do early starts particularly affect teenagers?

questions.explanation: The second paragraph links short sleep to concentration, mood, and illness.
options: Weaker concentration and more illness.
Stronger memory and better vision.
Faster growth and more energy.
Improved appetite and hearing.
questions.question: What effects of short sleep are mentioned?

questions.explanation: The final paragraph says buses, parents' hours, and sports all depend on current schedules.
options: Students refuse to sleep earlier.
Teachers dislike morning lessons.
Sleep has no effect on learning.
Transport and family routines depend on school times.
questions.question: What makes changing school start times difficult?

exercises.passage:
It Is Not Too Late

Adults who start learning a language often apologize for their age before the first lesson. Research offers encouragement: while children may master pronunciation more easily, adults learn grammar rules faster and bring stronger study habits. Motivation, not age, is usually the deciding factor.

The most common mistake is waiting too long to speak. Learners who spend months only on apps and word lists arrive at their first conversation unable to build a sentence under pressure. Short, regular speaking practice trains the mouth and the memory together. Even ten minutes describing your day aloud helps.

Consistency beats intensity. Thirty focused minutes every day builds more lasting skill than a single exhausting weekend session. A learner who accepts small daily progress, forgives missed days, and keeps speaking from the start will usually surprise themselves within a year.

questions.explanation: The first paragraph says adults learn grammar faster and have stronger study habits.
options: Adults memorize faster than children in every area.
Adults learn grammar faster and study more effectively.
Adults never need to practise speaking.
Adults should only learn with textbooks.
questions.question: What advantage do adult learners have?

questions.explanation: The passage says learners who delay speaking cannot build sentences under pressure.
options: Using language apps every day.
Studying grammar rules first.
Delaying speaking practice for months.
Describing your day aloud.
questions.question: What mistake does the writer warn against?

questions.explanation: The final paragraph states that daily focused minutes beat one exhausting weekend session.
options: Daily focused practice beats occasional long sessions.
Weekend study is the only method that works.
Missing one day ruins all progress.
Speaking practice should be avoided.
questions.question: What does the writer recommend about study habits?

exercises.passage:
Four Days, Same Pay?

Several large trials have tested a four-day working week with no cut in salary. The results surprised many managers: revenue stayed steady or rose, sick days fell, and most employees said they would not return to five days. With one extra day for rest and errands, people arrived on Monday with more energy.

The model demands discipline. Meetings get shorter and coffee breaks fewer; low-value tasks are simply dropped. Companies that failed usually failed here. They removed a working day without changing how the other four were used, so the same workload was squeezed into less time.

A four-day week is not possible everywhere. Hospitals, restaurants, and emergency services must cover every day, so they experiment instead with shorter shifts or flexible rotas. The broader lesson still applies: many organizations discover they can achieve the same results in less time once they measure output instead of hours.

questions.explanation: The first paragraph reports steady or rising revenue, fewer sick days, and higher energy.
options: Revenue always collapsed.
Employees demanded a return to five days.
Sick days increased sharply.
Revenue held steady while wellbeing improved.
questions.question: What did the trials generally find?

questions.explanation: The passage says failing companies removed a day without changing how the other four were used.
options: They paid employees too much.
They kept old work habits in fewer days.
They hired too many new managers.
They refused to hold any meetings.
questions.question: Why did some companies fail with the model?

questions.explanation: Hospitals and restaurants must cover every day, so they try shorter shifts or flexible rotas instead.
options: They already work only three days.
Their employees dislike short weeks.
They must stay open daily, so they adapt differently.
They are banned from any experiments.
questions.question: How do hospitals and restaurants handle the idea?

exercises.passage:
The First Step In

A first internship can feel disappointingly ordinary: answering emails, organizing files, and watching experienced colleagues do the interesting work. Yet these small tasks serve a purpose. They teach the unspoken rules of professional life: how meetings run, how deadlines are tracked, and how colleagues ask for help. No classroom fully explains these.

The difference between a useful internship and a wasted summer is usually mentoring. Interns who meet weekly with a supervisor to review progress learn far more than those left alone with repetitive tasks. A good mentor explains not just what to do but why it matters to the team.

Pay remains controversial. Unpaid positions exclude students who cannot afford to work for free, while paid programs attract stronger applicants and treat interns as real contributors. Whatever the salary, the true test of an internship is simple: does the intern leave with skills and contacts they did not have before?

questions.explanation: The first paragraph says small tasks teach the unspoken rules of professional life.
options: Small tasks teach the unspoken rules of work.
Emails are the most important skill in any job.
Interns should avoid watching colleagues.
Filing is more valuable than mentoring.
questions.question: What value do routine tasks have for interns?

questions.explanation: Weekly supervisor meetings to review progress separate useful internships from wasted ones.
options: Working completely alone.
Avoiding all feedback.
Regular mentoring and progress reviews.
Doing only the most exciting tasks.
questions.question: What makes an internship useful rather than wasted?

questions.explanation: The final paragraph asks whether the intern leaves with new skills and contacts.
options: The size of the company.
The length of the lunch break.
The number of emails answered.
New skills and contacts gained.
questions.question: What is the true test of an internship?

exercises.passage:
The Interview Is a Conversation

Many candidates treat job interviews as exams with right and wrong answers. Stronger candidates treat them as professional conversations. Researching the company beforehand, its products, customers, and recent news, allows an applicant to connect their own experience to real problems the team faces.

Stories beat adjectives. Saying 'I am a great team player' convinces nobody, but describing a disagreement you helped resolve shows teamwork in action. The best interview stories follow a simple shape: the situation, the action you took, and the result. One clear example usually impresses more than five vague claims.

Good interviews run both ways. Candidates who ask thoughtful questions about training, daily work, and how success is measured learn whether the job truly fits them. An interview that feels like a real discussion is often a sign of a workplace where communication works.

questions.explanation: Researching products, customers, and news lets applicants connect experience to real problems.
options: Memorizing the company's founding date.
Connecting your experience to the team's real problems.
Flattering every interviewer personally.
Asking for the highest possible salary first.
questions.question: Why should candidates research the company?

questions.explanation: The passage says one clear situation-action-result example beats five vague claims.
options: One clear example beats several vague claims.
Longer answers are always better.
Adjectives convince more than stories.
Results should never be mentioned.
questions.question: What does the writer say about interview stories?

questions.explanation: Asking about training, daily work, and success measures shows whether the job fits.
options: It guarantees a job offer.
It shows the candidate is desperate.
It reveals whether the job truly fits.
It shortens the interview unfairly.
questions.question: Why should candidates ask their own questions?

exercises.passage:
Someone Who Has Been There

Starting a first job can feel like arriving in a country where you do not speak the language. A workplace mentor, an experienced colleague assigned to guide newcomers, shortens this difficult period. Mentors explain procedures, introduce key people, and warn beginners about common mistakes before they happen.

The relationship benefits both sides. New employees settle faster and make fewer expensive errors, while mentors often report that explaining their work forces them to organize their own knowledge more clearly. Some even discover leadership ability they had not suspected in themselves.

Effective mentoring needs structure. Pairs who meet regularly with a simple agenda achieve more than those who only talk when problems appear. A short monthly conversation about goals, difficulties, and next steps keeps the relationship useful long after the nervous first weeks are over.

questions.explanation: Mentors explain procedures, introduce people, and warn about mistakes in advance.
options: They set salaries for newcomers.
They replace all formal training.
They evaluate beginners for dismissal.
They guide newcomers and warn about mistakes early.
questions.question: What does a workplace mentor do?

questions.explanation: Explaining their work forces mentors to organize their own knowledge more clearly.
options: Mentors receive automatic promotions.
Mentors clarify their own knowledge by explaining it.
Mentors no longer need to do their jobs.
Mentors avoid all responsibility for errors.
questions.question: How do mentors benefit?

questions.explanation: Regular meetings with a simple agenda beat only talking when problems appear.
options: Regular meetings with a simple agenda.
Talking only when problems appear.
Ending contact after the first week.
Meeting without any plan or goals.
questions.question: What makes mentoring effective?

exercises.passage:
Starting Over at Thirty-Five

Changing careers in your thirties can feel like throwing away a decade of effort. In practice, little is wasted: a teacher who becomes a trainer, or a nurse who moves into health technology, carries across communication skills, patience, and professional contacts. Experience transfers more often than people expect.

The practical barriers are real, however. Retraining usually means evening courses after full working days, and an entry-level salary in a new field may be lower than the old one. Successful changers plan for this gap by saving several months of expenses before resigning and by testing the new field first, through freelance projects, volunteering, or shadowing a professional for a week.

The deepest obstacle is often psychological. Admitting that a chosen path no longer fits can feel like failure, when it is really information. People who treat the move as a reversible, time-limited experiment adapt faster than those who demand a guarantee before the first step.

questions.explanation: The teacher and nurse examples show communication skills and contacts carrying across.
options: Previous experience is always completely useless.
Only young people can learn new skills.
Skills and contacts often transfer to the new field.
Employers never hire career changers.
questions.question: What does the passage say about past experience?

questions.explanation: The passage recommends saving months of expenses and testing the field first.
options: Save money in advance and test the new field first.
Resign immediately without any plan.
Refuse all freelance or volunteer work.
Avoid talking to professionals in the field.
questions.question: How should career changers handle the practical barriers?

questions.explanation: Treating the move as a reversible, time-limited experiment helps people adapt faster.
options: Wait for a guarantee before acting.
Treat the move as a reversible experiment.
Keep the decision secret from everyone.
Change fields every few months.
questions.question: What mindset helps most?
